extracted.intended_audience: general readers and privacy-conscious technologists (people organizing keysigning parties / learning web-of-trust practices)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical/social procedures and operational-security practices for generating keys, running a keysigning party, and seeding a web-of-trust so participants can vouch for one another. Includes invitation rules, key-generation steps, verification, and anti-surveillance precautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive trust / web of trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust that moves across the web of our relationships: if you trust someone and they sign a key for another person, that vouching transfers trust along the chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via keyrings: someone adds signed keys to their keyring and shares it; provided you trust the person who created the keyring, you can add those keys to yours. Emphasizes that trust is only valid so long as each link in the chain is trusted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keysigning parties to seed the web
rubrics_metrics.description: Keysigning parties are 'a party where everyone gets together and signs everyone else's keys' and are used to create the seed of the web of trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With more people the ring grows and expands as people meet others and add more names. Mini-keysigning (two people trading keys) is a micro-example; larger gatherings produce a more useful seed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invitation control and guest restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit attendance to trusted people to avoid infiltration or unnecessary exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original suggested messaging: 'Just tell them it's a super-private party, invitational only... Tell them not to bring anyone along or they won't be admitted.' Practical compromise used in the text: allow a maximum of one guest, and that guest must be someone the inviter has known personally for at least five years. Anti-pattern: bluntly forbidding guests tends to provoke people to bring extra friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a freshly-built, trusted machine (air-gapped / known-good media)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate keys on a machine you trust: rebuilt 'from the ground up', booted from a fresh ParanoidLinux DVD (or equivalent), and controlled by the event organizers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speaker: 'I trust this machine. Every component in it was laid by our own hands. It's running a fresh out-of-the-box version of ParanoidLinux, booted off of the DVD.' The implication is to minimize supply-chain or preinstalled compromise by using known-good media and hardware you control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate entropy locally and avoid persisting private keys
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants provide local randomness (mash keys, wiggle the mouse) to seed key generation; private keys are displayed and not stored on disk by the generator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process described: user gives random input, generator displays private key (user may photograph it), then the generator erases it ('hit any key to make it go away forever -- it's not stored on the disk at all'). This reduces risk of the generation environment retaining the private key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record public key ownership with photos and later convert carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a photo of the public-key display with the owner standing next to it so others can later be confident whose key it is; later transcribe the photos into actual key material on your own device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the event: 'you call over all the people here you trust and who trust you, and *they* take a picture of the screen with you standing next to it, so they know whose key it is.' Warning: transcription is 'a lot of work' and must be done carefully; 'one mistake and you're screwed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify typed-in keys via fingerprint comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the short fingerprint under the key as a checksum to ensure the typed-in key matches the displayed key.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: once you've typed in the key, generate a fingerprint from it and compare to the fingerprint shown at the event: 'if they match, you've got it right.' Emphasizes the fingerprint as the reliable low-cost verification method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delete photos of private/public-key displays after transcription
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove photographic traces of keys and participants after keys have been transcribed to avoid public evidence linking people to the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit admonition: '*Delete those photos once you've typed in the keys*!' Rationale: to avoid a Flickr stream or other online archive that could expose participants and their associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physically destroy generation hardware if compromise feared
rubrics_metrics.description: If there's any doubt about the trustworthiness of the generation machine, physically destroy it to eliminate any stored secrets or covert recording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by smashing the laptop with a hammer, exposing and destroying the hard drive, placing the remains in salt water. This is presented as an over-the-top but clear assurance against retained copies of keys or covert logging. Consider cost and practicality vs. threat level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess personal trustworthiness in person before signing
rubrics_metrics.description: Meet and evaluate people face-to-face to decide how much you can trust them before signing their keys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizer: 'Now what I want from you tonight is to meet the people here and figure out how much you can trust them.' The party's purpose includes social judgment: not everyone present must be known to you in advance, but you should decide whether to vouch for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume an active adversary (social engineering and infiltration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model the threat as including spies who will use social engineering to identify and entrap participants; operate accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text warns: 'We know that there are DHS spies who use it now. They use social engineering hacks to try to get us to reveal ourselves so that they can bust us.' Consequences: keep reasons secret, control invitations, and avoid admitting organizational leadership or affiliations at the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keyring handling and propagation
rubrics_metrics.description: How to use and share keyrings: add signed keys to your keyring and share keyrings only when you trust the original signer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained: 'I can put [a key] on my "keyring" -- a list of keys that I've signed with my private key. That means you can unlock it with my public key and know for sure that me -- or someone with my key, anyway -- says that "this key belongs to this guy."' Guidance emphasizes that when you accept a keyring from someone, you are implicitly trusting their vetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational-anonymity practices in daily life
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyday operational security measures to reduce traceability between identities and activities (examples given: cloning transit passes, avoiding issued IDs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative examples include: not using an issued Muni pass and cloning someone else's pass multiple times daily ('habitually cloned someone else's Muni pass three or four times a day, assuming a new identity for every ride'). These are presented as local practices to reduce linkage outside the keysigning context.
